attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his Where's Your Ed At post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will' with two alternatives. The proposition keeps both branches. The point about paying DeepSeek is left out, and the contract handles it correctly.

contract.note: Either branch is enough, which is the plain reading of the 'or'. Further training of DeepSeek's released distilled models counts as building on what DeepSeek created. No deadline was given, so a dated derivative release resolves the claim early.

evidence.note: Skywork's repo records the OR1 release on May 13, 2025, trained on DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. It is Skywork's own disclosure, but it documents a third-party derivative release.
The arXiv technical report from May 2025 confirms OR1 was built on the DeepSeek-R1-Distill series and that its weights were open-sourced.

reviews.rationale: Under the early-resolution rule, a dated third-party derivative release after January 29, 2025 settles the claim. The Skywork-OR1 release in May 2025, built on DeepSeek distilled models and backed by a technical report, meets the derivative-model branch. No counterevidence was found.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, made in his own voice.

semantics.note: Two present-tense observations: training data is running short, and capabilities had been peaking since March 2024. The proposition keeps both clauses.

contract.note: The plain readings are ordinary ones: a data constraint that is approaching, and broadly flattened capability progress. 'Peaking' is ambiguous and the contract flags this. Scoring each clause separately, with mixed allowed, is fair.

evidence.note: Epoch's June 2024 paper estimates the stock of usable public human text will be fully used around 2026 to 2032. That supports an approaching constraint, though not exhaustion.
ARC Prize's independent baseline from September 2024: o1-preview scored 21.2% against GPT-4o's 9%. That is progress after March, though at much higher inference time.
OpenAI's own results (a developer disclosure) show large o1-preview gains over GPT-4o on AIME, GPQA and coding in September 2024.
METR found limited autonomy gains for o1-preview, which shows progress was uneven. METR notes its tests may underestimate the model, so this does not establish a plateau.

reviews.rationale: The data clause holds: Epoch's research supports an approaching constraint on public human text. The capability clause fails: independent ARC Prize results and OpenAI's developer evaluations show substantial gains after March 2024 on several hard tasks. METR shows the gains were uneven but not flat. Per the contract, this is mixed.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, made in his own voice.

semantics.note: Two universal negatives: no trillion-dollar problems solved, and no profitable outcomes for any business. The tone is polemical, but the profitability part can be tested. The proposition is faithful.

contract.note: Calendar 2024 is a window the evaluator chose, but a reasonable one. Requiring net attributable profit is an ordinary reading of 'profitable'. 'Trillion-dollar problems' has no valuation basis, which the contract flags.

evidence.note: Klarna's own claim of about SEK 100m in annualized AI marketing savings. These are gross, annualized and not reconciled against costs, so they do not show realized net deployment profit.

reviews.rationale: The packet has only Klarna's annualized gross savings claim, which does not meet the contract's bar for realized net profit. Nothing in the packet shows a trillion-dollar problem solved. Not finding a counterexample does not prove the universal negatives, so the packet settles neither limb.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, made in his own voice.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim about hyperscalers' leverage and Microsoft's licence rights. The revision correctly drops the DeepSeek framing that came from the preceding rhetorical question. 'Hold all the cards' is partly rhetoric.

contract.note: Reading the claim as practical capacity and contractual freedom, with 'non-revocable' and 'unfettered' tested as separate licence assertions, is ordinary. The January 2025 window is the evaluator's choice, but reasonable.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own January 21, 2025 statement shows rights to OpenAI IP through 2030. It supports substantial access only. It does not establish irrevocability or unfettered use, and its 'within our products' wording suggests a limited scope.
OpenAI's October 2025 announcement describes later changes to the terms. That period falls outside the target window, so it cannot establish the January restrictions.

reviews.rationale: The evidence confirms Microsoft had substantial access to OpenAI IP in January 2025. It does not show the licences were non-revocable or unfettered, or that hyperscalers faced no material barriers to replacing GPT and Claude. The October 2025 terms are outside the period. The packet does not settle the claim.
